The rapidity of convergence on Ratzinger in four ballots — reaching the 77-vote threshold comfortably on the fourth — was interpreted as an expression of strong if not unanimous consensus.
The Announcement

At 5:50 PM CEST on April 19, white smoke rose from the Sistine Chapel chimney, signaling the election of a new pope. About 53 minutes later, at 6:43 PM, Cardinal Jorge Medina Estévez, Protodeacon of the College of Cardinals, appeared on the central balcony of St. Peter’s Basilica and announced in Latin: “Annuntio vobis gaudium magnum: Habemus Papam” (“I announce to you a great joy: We have a pope”), followed by the new pope’s identity: “Eminentissimum ac Reverendissimum Dominum, Dominum Iosephum, Sanctae Romanae Ecclesiae Cardinalem Ratzinger, qui sibi nomen imposuit Benedictum XVI”. An estimated 150,000–200,000 people in St. Peter’s Square received the announcement; the worldwide television audience exceeded 1 billion.
Benedict XVI’s Background and Theological Profile

Joseph Aloisius Ratzinger was born on April 16, 1927, in Marktl am Inn, Bavaria, Germany — the son of a gendarmerie officer. His early life was shadowed by the Third Reich: he was briefly conscripted into the Hitler Youth (membership was legally compulsory by 1941) and served in an anti-aircraft unit, deserting in the war’s final days. He was ordained a Catholic priest in 1951 alongside his brother Georg.

Ratzinger was a peritus (expert theologian) at the Second Vatican Council (1962–1965) and initially embraced many of its reforms. He became Archbishop of Munich and Freising in 1977 and was made a cardinal the same year. His appointment as Prefect of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith in 1981 — the Vatican’s doctrinal watchdog, formerly known as the Holy Office (the Inquisition) — marked his transformation into the leading theological conservative in Church leadership. Over 24 years in that role, he issued disciplinary measures against liberation theologians (Leonardo Boff, Gustavo Gutiérrez), silenced theologians who departed from official teaching on contraception and homosexuality, and oversaw the drafting of the Catechism of the Catholic Church (1992). He earned the nickname “God’s Rottweiler” among critics and “the Pope’s enforcer” in the press for his uncompromising doctrinal positions.

His election was thus a deliberate choice by the College of Cardinals for intellectual rigor and doctrinal continuity at a moment when the Church faced mounting challenges from secularization in Europe, abuse scandals in several countries, and internal pressure for reform of teachings on contraception, clerical celibacy, and the ordination of women.
Inauguration and First Papal Acts
The Inaugural Mass

Benedict XVI’s papal inauguration Mass on April 24, 2005, was attended by an estimated 350,000 faithful in St. Peter’s Square and broadcast to an estimated 1 billion viewers. Notable attendees included German Chancellor Gerhard Schröder, Spanish King Juan Carlos I and Queen Sofía, and British Prince Philip (representing Queen Elizabeth II). The ceremony was deliberately styled as an “inauguration” (Latin inauguratio) rather than a “coronation” — a distinction first made by John Paul I in 1978 — to signal collegial, servant leadership rather than monarchical authority. Benedict was invested with the pallium and Ring of the Fisherman but wore a mitre rather than the traditional triple-crowned papal tiara, which had not been used since Paul VI placed it on the altar of St. Peter’s as a symbolic renunciation in 1964.

His inaugural homily emphasized three recurring themes: that the Church is “alive” because Christ is alive; the “co-responsibility” of all baptized Christians; and his intention to open dialogue with “brothers and sisters of the Jewish world” and other Christian denominations. The speech was delivered in Italian and conducted partly in Latin, signaling both modern accessibility and liturgical continuity.
Early Governance
In his first months, Benedict XVI made several notable appointments and declarations:
June 2005: He convened a Synod of Bishops on the Eucharist for October 2005, continuing John Paul II’s late-pontificate emphasis on Eucharistic theology.

August 2005: He hosted World Youth Day in Cologne, Germany (August 18–21), drawing an estimated 800,000–1,000,000 young Catholics — the first World Youth Day in his homeland. His homily there emphasized dialogue with Islam in the context of the July 7 London bombings (see 7/7 London bombings).
September 2005: He received Israeli President Moshe Katsav in a private audience, a significant symbolic step in Jewish-Catholic relations, and expressed his “immense sorrow” for the Shoah.

November 2005: He issued a significant document on homosexuality and seminary admissions (Instruction Concerning the Criteria for the Discernment of Vocations with regard to Persons with Homosexual Tendencies), barring the ordination of men with “deep-seated homosexual tendencies.”
Deus Caritas Est — First Encyclical

On December 25, 2005, Pope Benedict XVI signed his first encyclical, Deus Caritas Est (“God Is Love”), officially promulgated on January 25, 2006, on the feast of the Conversion of St. Paul. The document was published in eight languages simultaneously and became one of his most widely read writings.
The encyclical is structured in two parts:

Part I — The Unity of Love in Creation and in Salvation History: Ratzinger examined the Greek words eros (romantic/passionate love) and agape (self-giving love), arguing against the caricature that Christianity denigrated bodily love. He asserted that eros and agape are not opposed but are transformed when ordered toward their divine source: “Even if eros is at first mainly covetous and ascending, a fascination for the great promise of happiness, in drawing near to the other, it is less and less concerned with itself, increasingly seeks the happiness of the other, is concerned more and more with the beloved, bestows itself and wants to ‘be there for’ the other.”

Part II — The Church’s Charitable Activity: The second half addressed caritas — the Church’s practical charitable mission — and the proper relationship between ecclesial charity and political action. Benedict distinguished the Church’s role (creating just conditions of the heart; supporting the poor through love) from the state’s role (creating just legal and social structures). The document argued that the Church’s charitable organizations (Caritas Internationalis, local charitable works) must remain distinct from political advocacy.

The encyclical was praised even by secular critics for its philosophical depth and lyrical prose. The New York Times described it as “surprisingly warm and personal” compared to what many expected from a pope known for doctrinal severity. It remains one of the most-cited papal documents of the early twenty-first century.
Conclave Dynamics and Long-Term Succession

The 2005 conclave generated significant historical significance beyond Benedict’s election itself. Cardinal Jorge Mario Bergoglio of Buenos Aires, Argentina, received the second-highest vote count — approximately 35 votes on the second ballot, declining to approximately 26 by the fourth as the conclave consolidated around Ratzinger. Bergoglio, a Jesuit known for pastoral simplicity and engagement with urban poverty, represented a markedly different vision of Church leadership. His 2013 election as Pope Francis — following Benedict’s unprecedented voluntary resignation on February 28, 2013 — created a living contrast between two popes and two ecclesial visions that defined Catholic discourse throughout the 2010s.

Cardinal Carlo Maria Martini of Milan (since retired to Jerusalem for study) had long been considered a possible “reform” candidate but declined to campaign; he received approximately 9–12 votes on the first ballot before withdrawing. Martini died in 2012, leaving an influential posthumous interview in which he described the Church as “200 years behind” on questions of sexuality and ethics.
Reception and International Reaction
Reaction to Benedict’s election divided along predictable lines:

Germany: Widespread national pride; front pages across the country celebrated the first German pope in a millennium. “We are pope” (Wir sind Papst) was the famous headline of German tabloid Bild, which captured the national sentiment.

Progressive Catholics: Deep concern about doctrinal rigidity; liberal Catholic groups in the United States, Germany, and the Netherlands called for dialogue on contraception, clerical celibacy, and women’s ordination.

Jewish organizations: Initial anxiety about Ratzinger’s record, specifically his 2000 document Dominus Iesus, which reasserted that salvation was uniquely mediated through the Catholic Church. His September audience with Israeli President Katsav partially addressed this.
Ecumenical partners: Measured welcome from Protestant and Orthodox leaders, who noted Benedict’s stated commitment to Christian unity while acknowledging his conservative starting point.
Time magazine included Benedict XVI in its April 2005 list of the 100 Most Influential People in the World — an accolade conferred the week of his election.
Significance

Pope Benedict XVI’s election and early papacy in 2005 marked a pivotal moment for global Catholicism at a juncture when the Church faced multiple converging pressures: secularization in its European heartland, the legacy of clerical abuse scandals, and theological debates that had simmered since Vatican II. His election represented a deliberate choice for doctrinal continuity and intellectual rigour over pastoral innovation, signaling that the majority of the College of Cardinals — shaped by John Paul II’s appointments over 26 years — prioritized doctrinal clarity.

At the same time, Benedict’s Deus Caritas Est complicated easy caricatures of his papacy: his first systematic statement to the world was a meditation on love, charity, and the Church’s humanitarian mission, not a doctrinal condemnation. The combination suggested a more complex figure than his CDF reputation implied.

His resignation in 2013 — the first by a reigning pope since Gregory XII in 1415, nearly 600 years — proved to be his most historically unprecedented act, and it directly enabled the election of Francis, the very conclave alternative who had come second to him in 2005. The 2005 conclave thus shaped Catholic history not once but twice: immediately, in electing Benedict, and eight years later, in making possible the papacy that would succeed him.

text: Key figures: Pope John Paul II (Karol Józef Wojtyła), Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger (Pope Benedict XVI)
Summary

Pope John Paul II, born Karol Józef Wojtyła in Wadowice, Poland, in 1920, died on April 2, 2005, at the age of 84 in his private apartment in the Apostolic Palace at Vatican City. Elected on October 16, 1978, he had been the first non-Italian pope since Adrian VI in the 16th century, and his roughly 26-year reign ranks among the longest in the history of the papacy. His health had declined for years amid Parkinson’s disease, and his final illness drew sustained worldwide attention.

His funeral, held on April 8, 2005, was one of the largest gatherings of Christians in history, with an estimated four million mourners converging on Rome and roughly one million filing past his body as it lay in state in St. Peter’s Basilica. Numerous heads of state attended, including U.S. President George W. Bush and Polish President Aleksander Kwaśniewski.

The papal conclave to choose his successor convened on April 18, 2005, with 115 cardinal electors meeting in the Sistine Chapel. After four ballots over two days, Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger was elected on April 19, 2005, and took the name Benedict XVI. John Paul II was beatified on May 1, 2011, and canonized as Saint John Paul II by Pope Francis on April 27, 2014.
Significance

John Paul II’s papacy reshaped the modern Roman Catholic Church and the broader global stage. He is widely credited with helping to undermine communist rule in his native Poland and across Eastern Europe, and he became the most-traveled pope in history, dramatically expanding the Church’s global presence through pastoral visits and outreach. His death and funeral marked an unusually large international moment of mourning, and the swift conclave that followed underscored the institutional continuity of the papacy as Benedict XVI inherited his legacy.

text: Key figures: Prince Charles (Prince of Wales), Camilla Parker Bowles, Queen Elizabeth II, Archbishop of Canterbury Rowan Williams
Summary

On April 9, 2005, Prince Charles, heir to the British throne, married Camilla Parker Bowles in a two-part ceremony at Windsor, England. The civil marriage took place at Windsor Guildhall with limited attendance—restricted to close family members, notably excluding Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip—before transitioning to a Service of Prayer and Dedication at St George’s Chapel, Windsor Castle, where approximately 800 guests witnessed the blessing. The ceremony was witnessed by Prince William and Prince Harry (Charles’s sons) and Tom Parker Bowles (Camilla’s son). The attendees included senior members of the royal family, foreign royalty, British political leaders including Prime Minister Tony Blair, religious figures led by Archbishop of Canterbury Rowan Williams, and notable public figures such as Stephen Fry and Rowan Atkinson. Camilla wore a cream dress and coat designed by Robinson Valentine with a Philip Treacy hat, and the couple exchanged rings fashioned from Welsh gold from the Clogau St David’s mine. The BBC broadcast the ceremony live to approximately 7.3 million viewers. The Queen hosted a reception at Windsor Castle following the Service, and the couple honeymooned at Birkhall on the Balmoral Estate.
Background

Charles and Camilla first met in 1970 and had maintained a relationship, with varying degrees of publicity, across nearly four decades. Charles married Lady Diana Spencer on July 29, 1981, in a ceremony at St Paul’s Cathedral watched by an estimated 750 million television viewers worldwide. That marriage ended in divorce in August 1996, and Diana died in a Paris car crash on August 31, 1997. Camilla had herself been married to Brigadier Andrew Parker Bowles from 1973 to 1995.

Public and institutional resistance to the relationship was substantial throughout the 1990s, driven in part by Diana’s documented unhappiness and the sympathetic public narrative around her. By the early 2000s, however, opinion polls showed a gradual softening: a 2004 survey found around 65% of Britons supportive of the marriage, provided Camilla did not become Queen. The Church of England’s own General Synod had ruled in 2002 that remarriage after divorce was permissible in exceptional circumstances, clearing the canonical obstacle that had long been cited as a barrier.
The postponement

The wedding had originally been scheduled for April 8, 2005, but was moved back by one day after the state funeral of Pope John Paul II was confirmed for that date at St Peter’s Basilica in Rome. Prince Charles attended the Pope’s funeral on April 8; the Vatican ceremony drew more than 200 heads of state and government in what was described as one of the largest gatherings of world leaders in history. The rescheduling required fresh legal paperwork, as the registrar’s licence was date-specific, and prompted a brief public exchange between Clarence House and Windsor Borough Council.
The ceremony in detail

The civil ceremony at Windsor Guildhall lasted approximately twenty minutes and was open only to around 30 close family members. Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip chose not to attend the civil register ceremony—Buckingham Palace indicated the Queen wished to host the subsequent reception rather than participate in both events—though they were both present for the religious blessing at St George’s Chapel.

At St George’s Chapel the Service of Prayer and Dedication was conducted by the Archbishop of Canterbury, Rowan Williams. In a striking gesture of transparency, both Charles and Camilla publicly recited a general confession from the 1662 Book of Common Prayer acknowledging their “manifold sins and wickedness”—a passage described by commentators as the most candid act of penitence ever performed publicly by senior royals. The service lasted about 45 minutes.

Camilla’s title upon marriage became HRH The Duchess of Cornwall for most purposes in the United Kingdom; in Scotland she was known as the Duchess of Rothesay. Clarence House announced that, should Charles become king, she intended to be known as Princess Consort rather than Queen Consort—a distinction later reversed: when Charles acceded to the throne as King Charles III in September 2022, Camilla became Queen Consort and was crowned alongside him at Westminster Abbey on May 6, 2023.

The couple’s wedding rings were fashioned from Welsh gold, continuing a royal tradition dating to 1923, when the future Queen Elizabeth The Queen Mother’s wedding ring was made from gold mined at the Clogau St David’s mine near Dolgellau. Gold from the same Welsh source has been used for royal wedding rings across subsequent generations.
Media and public reaction

Television audiences in the United Kingdom peaked at approximately 7.3 million for the BBC live broadcast, considerably below the 28 million who watched Charles and Diana’s 1981 wedding. An estimated 20,000 well-wishers lined Windsor’s streets on the day. International coverage was extensive: American networks including NBC, ABC, CBS, and CNN carried live or same-day footage.

Opinion polling conducted in the days following the wedding showed around 60% of British respondents supportive of the marriage, while a minority—particularly among older age groups—continued to express reservations. The wedding received broadly positive coverage in the Commonwealth realms, though media in Australia and Canada noted the absence of Prime Ministers from either country among the 800 guests.
Significance

The wedding marked a historic moment for the British monarchy and the culmination of a relationship spanning decades. Charles’s marriage to Camilla, following his 1981–1996 marriage to Diana and the public controversy surrounding his post-Diana relationship with Camilla, represented a significant shift in royal precedent and public acceptance. The event demonstrated the monarchy’s capacity to adapt ceremonial and religious practices to contemporary circumstances.

The 2005 wedding occurred within a year dense with consequential events for European heads of state: Pope John Paul II died two weeks before the ceremony, and Pope Benedict XVI was elected just ten days after. In July, Prime Minister Tony Blair—who had attended the Windsor reception—faced the immediate aftermath of the 7 July London bombings before hosting the G8 summit at Gleneagles.

text: Key figures: Saddam Hussein (former President of Iraq), Rizgar Mohammed Amin (chief judge), Barzan Ibrahim al-Tikriti (co-defendant, former intelligence chief), Taha Yassin Ramadan (co-defendant, former Vice President), Awad Hamed al-Bandar (co-defendant, former chief judge of the Revolutionary Court)
Summary

On 19 October 2005, the trial of Saddam Hussein, the former President of Iraq deposed during the 2003 U.S.-led invasion, opened before the Iraqi Special Tribunal in Baghdad. Saddam and seven co-defendants faced charges of crimes against humanity arising from the al-Dujail case — the killing of 148 Shia men and boys from the town of Dujail in retaliation for a failed assassination attempt against Saddam on 8 July 1982. All eight defendants pleaded not guilty before Chief Judge Rizgar Mohammed Amin. The proceeding was the first of several planned prosecutions of the former Iraqi leader and marked the opening of one of the most closely watched trials of the decade.
Background

Saddam Hussein had ruled Iraq from 1979 until his government was toppled by the U.S.-led coalition in April 2003. He was captured by American forces near his hometown of Tikrit on 13 December 2003 and held in custody while Iraqi and coalition authorities prepared to prosecute him. The Iraqi Special Tribunal — later renamed the Supreme Iraqi Criminal Tribunal, and often referred to as the Iraqi High Tribunal — had been established in December 2003 to try members of the former regime for genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes.

Prosecutors chose to try the comparatively well-documented al-Dujail case first. In July 1982, after gunmen fired on Saddam’s motorcade in the mainly Shia town of Dujail, north of Baghdad, the regime responded with mass arrests, torture, and executions; orchards were razed and 148 townspeople were sentenced to death. Building the case around a single, documented incident was intended to yield a manageable prosecution ahead of larger charges, including the Anfal campaign against Iraq’s Kurds.
The Proceedings

At the opening session on 19 October 2005, Saddam and his co-defendants entered not-guilty pleas. Alongside Saddam, the accused included his half-brother Barzan Ibrahim al-Tikriti, the former head of the intelligence service; Taha Yassin Ramadan, a former Vice President; Awad Hamed al-Bandar, former chief judge of the Revolutionary Court; and four lower-ranking Baath Party officials from Dujail. Saddam repeatedly questioned the legitimacy of the court and at times refused to recognise its authority.

The trial was marked by disruption and violence. The day after it opened, defence lawyer Saadoun Sughaiyer al-Janabi was abducted and killed; a second defence attorney, Adel al-Zubeidi, was assassinated on 8 November 2005, and Saddam’s chief defence lawyer, Khamis al-Obeidi, was later killed in June 2006. Amid frequent walkouts, hunger strikes, and outbursts in the courtroom, Chief Judge Rizgar Amin resigned in January 2006, citing government interference and public criticism that he had been too lenient. He was succeeded by Raouf Abdul Rahman, who imposed stricter control over the proceedings.
Verdict and Aftermath

The al-Dujail trial concluded in July 2006, and on 5 November 2006 the tribunal found Saddam Hussein guilty of crimes against humanity and sentenced him to death by hanging. An appeals chamber upheld the sentence on 26 December 2006, and Saddam was executed on 30 December 2006. Co-defendants Barzan al-Tikriti and Awad al-Bandar were also sentenced to death and executed in January 2007.

The trial drew sustained criticism from international observers. Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International, and United Nations bodies argued that the tribunal fell short of international fair-trial standards, pointing to the killings of defence lawyers, the mid-trial replacement of the presiding judge, and political interference in the process. Supporters countered that an Iraqi court trying a former Iraqi ruler on Iraqi soil represented an assertion of national sovereignty and accountability.
Significance

Saddam Hussein’s trial was a defining episode of post-invasion Iraq, offering a public accounting of the former regime’s abuses while exposing the fragility of Iraq’s new legal institutions amid an intensifying insurgency. It was one of the first instances of a deposed head of state being tried by a domestic court of his own country for crimes against humanity, and it fuelled a lasting debate over how to balance justice, due process, and legitimacy in transitional societies. The proceedings, and Saddam’s execution fourteen months later, became enduring symbols of the contested legacy of the Iraq War.

text: Key figures: Samuel Alito Jr., George W. Bush, Sandra Day O’Connor, Harriet Miers, Harry Reid, Arlen Specter, Patrick Leahy
The O’Connor Vacancy

On July 1, 2005, Justice Sandra Day O’Connor — the first woman ever appointed to the Supreme Court and the decisive swing vote on dozens of landmark rulings — announced her retirement effective upon the confirmation of her successor. O’Connor’s departure opened the most consequential vacancy on the Court since Ruth Bader Ginsburg’s 1993 appointment. Because O’Connor had repeatedly cast the deciding vote in 5–4 decisions on abortion, affirmative action, and religious freedom, her successor would reshape the Court’s balance, not merely add to it.

President Bush moved quickly. On September 6, 2005, he elevated D.C. Circuit Judge John G. Roberts Jr. — originally nominated to fill O’Connor’s seat — to the Chief Justice vacancy created by William Rehnquist’s death on September 3. Roberts was confirmed 78–22 on September 29, 2005. The O’Connor seat now required a fresh nominee.
The Harriet Miers Detour

On October 3, 2005, President Bush stunned Washington by nominating Harriet Miers — his White House Counsel and personal attorney — to replace O’Connor. Miers had never served as a judge and had no public record of constitutional jurisprudence. The nomination drew immediate fire from an unexpected quarter: conservative legal scholars and Republican senators who had spent years building the Federalist Society’s bench and wanted a nominee with a proven originalist record. Weekly Standard editor William Kristol called the pick “a failure of nerve,” and former Reagan official Bruce Fein warned the Senate to reject her.

Democrats attacked from the other direction, citing Miers’s close personal relationship with Bush as disqualifying cronyism — a charge especially resonant days after Hurricane Katrina had exposed the consequences of “heckuva job” appointments. After a disastrous and widely mocked questionnaire submission to the Judiciary Committee, Miers withdrew on October 27, 2005, marking one of the rare instances of a presidential nominee collapsing before formal hearings began.
Alito’s Nomination

Four days later, on October 31, 2005, President Bush nominated U.S. Court of Appeals Judge Samuel Anthony Alito Jr. to fill the O’Connor vacancy. Alito, 55, had served on the Third Circuit since 1990 — appointed by President George H.W. Bush — and had authored over 300 opinions in fifteen years on the bench. His record was extensive and unambiguous: he had voted to uphold a Pennsylvania law requiring married women to notify their husbands before obtaining an abortion (Planned Parenthood v. Casey, 1991 Third Circuit panel), dissented in favor of police officers in excessive-force cases, and written opinions limiting the scope of the Family and Medical Leave Act.

Alito quickly earned the nickname “Scalito” in the press — a portmanteau referencing Justice Antonin Scalia — though Alito’s temperament in oral argument was widely described as quieter and more methodical than Scalia’s combativeness.
Judicial Philosophy

Alito was a committed textualist and originalist, approaching constitutional interpretation through the text and historical understanding of provisions at the time of their adoption. Unlike some nominees who cultivated studied ambiguity about their legal views, Alito’s Third Circuit tenure left a traceable paper trail on virtually every major constitutional question. His 1985 job application to the Justice Department stated that he was “particularly proud” of his work arguing that “the Constitution does not protect a right to an abortion” — a document that became central to Democratic opposition during hearings.
Confirmation Battle

The Judiciary Committee opened confirmation hearings on January 9, 2006, chaired by Senator Arlen Specter (R-PA). Alito appeared before the committee over four days, answering — or deferring — questions from all eighteen senators. Following the precedent set by Robert Bork’s disastrous 1987 hearings, modern nominees routinely declined to pre-commit on specific cases; Alito told the committee he would approach every case with an “open mind” and evaluate precedents under stare decisis. On abortion, he acknowledged that Roe v. Wade was settled precedent but declined to call it “super precedent” immune from reconsideration.

The hearing’s most dramatic moment came when Senator Lindsey Graham (R-SC) asked Alito whether he was “a bigot.” Alito’s wife, Martha-Ann Bomgardner, broke into tears and left the room — an image that dominated news coverage and shifted media narrative away from Democratic questioning on abortion and executive power. Democratic senators Ted Kennedy and Joe Biden faced criticism for lengthy speeches that left little time for follow-up.

The Judiciary Committee voted 10–8 along strict party lines on January 24, 2006, recommending confirmation. The full Senate confirmed Alito 58–42 on January 31, 2006, with only four Democrats — Robert Byrd (D-WV), Tim Johnson (D-SD), Kent Conrad (D-ND), and Ben Nelson (D-NE) — crossing party lines to vote in favor. A cloture vote the day before had broken a Democratic filibuster attempt 72–25. With only four members of the opposing party in support, Alito’s confirmation was among the most closely divided along party lines in modern Supreme Court history — a sharper partisan split than the 52–48 confirmation of Clarence Thomas in 1991, which drew eleven Democratic votes.
Significance

Alito’s confirmation completed a decisive transformation of the Court. Together with Chief Justice Roberts, confirmed in September, Bush had placed two solidly conservative justices on the bench in a single year. The pair — paired with Scalia, Thomas, and eventually Kennedy — formed a five-justice conservative bloc that would prove durable. Alito’s replacement of O’Connor was particularly consequential: where O’Connor’s swing-vote jurisprudence had produced narrow, fact-specific majorities, Alito reliably joined the conservative bloc and frequently authored its reasoning.

By the 2006–07 term, the Court signaled its new direction. In Gonzales v. Carhart (2007), Alito joined the majority upholding the federal Partial-Birth Abortion Ban Act — a law O’Connor had voted to strike down in similar form. In Ledbetter v. Goodyear (2007), Alito wrote the majority opinion restricting pay-discrimination claims, which Congress reversed with the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act of 2009.

The 2005 confirmation battle set the template for all subsequent Supreme Court fights: ideology, not qualifications, would determine Senate votes; nominees would decline to preview their legal views; and outside advocacy organizations would mobilize hundreds of millions of dollars on both sides. Sixteen years after his confirmation, Alito authored the Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization majority opinion (2022), directly overruling Roe v. Wade — reflecting the concerns Democrats had raised during his 2006 hearings.

text: Key figures: Askar Akayev (ousted President of Kyrgyzstan), Kurmanbek Bakiyev (opposition leader and interim head of state), Felix Kulov (opposition figure released during the uprising), Roza Otunbayeva (interim foreign minister)
Summary

The Tulip Revolution was a wave of popular protest in the spring of 2005 that toppled President Askar Akayev, who had governed Kyrgyzstan since the country’s independence from the Soviet Union in 1991. The unrest was triggered by parliamentary elections held on 27 February and 13 March 2005 that opposition groups and international monitors — notably the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) — condemned as marred by fraud, alongside long-standing grievances over corruption and authoritarian rule by Akayev’s family and allies.

Demonstrations began in the southern cities of Jalal-Abad and Osh before spreading north to the capital, Bishkek. On 24 March 2005 protesters stormed the main government headquarters, known as the White House, and Akayev fled the country the same day, travelling first to Kazakhstan and then to Russia. Three people died in the unrest, and mobs looted stores and cash machines in Bishkek as the government collapsed.

An interim administration led by the opposition figure Kurmanbek Bakiyev took power, naming him acting president and prime minister. Akayev signed a formal resignation at the Kyrgyz embassy in Moscow on 4 April 2005, and the interim parliament accepted it on 11 April. In a presidential election on 10 July 2005, Bakiyev won by a landslide, taking roughly 89 percent of the vote.
Background

Askar Akayev, a physicist who had led Kyrgyzstan since 1990, was once regarded as the most reform-minded leader in post-Soviet Central Asia, but by 2005 his rule was widely associated with corruption, nepotism, and the concentration of economic power within his family. The parliamentary elections of February and March 2005 became the immediate flashpoint: opposition candidates were disqualified or defeated in contests that observers judged neither free nor fair, and several members of Akayev’s family secured seats. The pattern echoed the disputed votes that had preceded earlier post-Soviet uprisings.
The Uprising

Protests first gathered force in the southern strongholds of Jalal-Abad and Osh in mid-March, where demonstrators seized regional administrative buildings. The opposition leader Kurmanbek Bakiyev, head of the People’s Movement of Kyrgyzstan, aligned himself with the protesters. On 24 March 2005 the demonstrations reached Bishkek, and crowds overran the presidential and government complex. Akayev and Prime Minister Nikolay Tanayev fled rather than order a violent crackdown, and the seat of government fell with little resistance. In the confusion, looting broke out across the capital and three people were killed. The imprisoned opposition figure Felix Kulov was freed and briefly placed in charge of security, while Roza Otunbayeva took over as interim foreign minister.
Aftermath

The interim leadership designated Bakiyev acting prime minister and then acting head of state pending a new election. Akayev negotiated the terms of his departure from Moscow, signing his resignation on 4 April 2005; it was ratified by the interim parliament on 11 April. Bakiyev consolidated his position by agreeing to run for president with Kulov as his prime minister, and on 10 July 2005 he won the presidency with about 89 percent of the vote. The alliance and the political settlement it produced proved unstable, and Kyrgyzstan experienced renewed upheaval later in the decade, including a second revolution that removed Bakiyev himself in 2010.
Significance

The Tulip Revolution was the third of the so-called “colour revolutions” that reshaped the post-Soviet space in the mid-2000s, following Georgia’s Rose Revolution of 2003 and Ukraine’s Orange Revolution of 2004. It was the first such movement to unseat a government in Central Asia, a region otherwise dominated by entrenched authoritarian rulers, and it demonstrated that mass mobilisation over a disputed election could bring down a long-serving president. Unlike the largely disciplined demonstrations in Tbilisi and Kyiv, the Kyrgyz revolt was marked by looting and disorder, and its outcome — a swift transfer of power to a new leader who soon faced the same accusations of corruption and authoritarianism — tempered contemporary hopes that it heralded durable democratisation. The events nonetheless established a pattern of street-led political change in Kyrgyzstan that recurred in 2010 and 2020.

text: Key figures: Tony Blair (Prime Minister, Labour leader), Michael Howard (Conservative leader), Charles Kennedy (Liberal Democrat leader), Gordon Brown (Chancellor of the Exchequer)
Summary

The 2005 United Kingdom general election was held on May 5, 2005. Tony Blair’s Labour Party won a third consecutive term in government—the first time a Labour leader had achieved three successive majority governments—but with a sharply reduced mandate. Labour took 355 of the 646 seats in the House of Commons on 35.2% of the popular vote, the lowest share ever recorded for a party forming a single-party majority government. Its overall majority fell from 167 to 66. The Conservatives under Michael Howard won 198 seats and 32.4% of the vote, and the Liberal Democrats under Charles Kennedy won 62 seats and 22.0%, their best result since the 1920s. National turnout was 61.4%.
Background

Labour had governed since Tony Blair’s landslide victory of 1997 and had won a second landslide in 2001. By 2005 the political climate had cooled markedly. The 2003 invasion of Iraq, undertaken over large-scale public protest and later controversy over the government’s case for war, had eroded trust in Blair personally and divided Labour’s traditional support. Domestic debates over public-service reform, university tuition fees, immigration, and asylum policy also shaped the campaign.

Michael Howard, who had become Conservative leader in 2003, sought to rebuild a party that had suffered two heavy defeats, campaigning on immigration controls, crime, and “cleaner hospitals.” Charles Kennedy’s Liberal Democrats positioned themselves to Labour’s left on several issues, opposing the Iraq war and university top-up fees, and targeting disaffected Labour voters as well as Conservative-held seats.
The election

Polling took place on May 5, 2005, for all 646 seats of the House of Commons. Labour’s vote share fell 5.5 percentage points from 2001 to 35.2%, and it lost dozens of seats, yet Britain’s first-past-the-post system converted its plurality into a working majority of 66. The Conservatives gained seats to reach 198 but were held below one-third of the national vote. The Liberal Democrats advanced to 62 seats, benefiting from anti-war sentiment and opposition to tuition fees.

The result was widely read as a rebuke delivered without a change of government: voters returned Labour to power while stripping away much of the authority it had enjoyed since 1997. Blair acknowledged on election night that the electorate had sent a message over Iraq and pledged to focus on domestic priorities.
Aftermath

Michael Howard announced shortly after the election that he would resign as Conservative leader once a successor could be chosen; the ensuing contest was won by David Cameron in December 2005. Charles Kennedy remained Liberal Democrat leader until January 2006. Blair had stated before the election that he would serve a full third term but would not seek a fourth; the reduced majority intensified pressure within Labour over the timing of his departure and the succession of Chancellor Gordon Brown, to whom Blair handed the premiership in June 2007.
Significance

The 2005 election confirmed Labour’s dominance of British politics across three parliaments while exposing the limits of that dominance. Blair’s third victory secured his place as Labour’s most electorally successful leader, but the 35.2% vote share—smaller than that of any previous single-party majority government—underscored how far his personal standing and the party’s coalition had narrowed since 1997. The gap between vote share and seat share renewed debate over the fairness of the first-past-the-post electoral system.

The election also reset the opposition. The Conservatives’ recovery was modest, and Howard’s resignation opened the way for David Cameron’s modernising leadership, which would carry the party back toward government by 2010. For Blair, the diminished mandate framed a difficult final period in office: within two months he was managing the response to the 7 July London bombings and hosting the G8 summit at Gleneagles, which opened the day after London won the 2012 Olympic bid.

text: Key figures: Condoleezza Rice, George W. Bush, Colin Powell, Senator Barbara Boxer (lead opponent during confirmation)
Summary

Condoleezza Rice was confirmed as the 66th U.S. Secretary of State on January 26, 2005, succeeding Colin Powell in President George W. Bush’s second term. The Senate voted 85–13 in her favor, making it the most opposition votes cast against a Secretary of State nominee in decades. Born on November 14, 1954, in Birmingham, Alabama, Rice became the first African American woman to hold the position — the second African American (after Powell) and the second woman (after Madeleine Albright, 1997–2001). Her appointment marked a significant milestone in American diplomatic history.

Rice had served as National Security Advisor since January 2001, guiding Bush’s foreign policy through the September 11 attacks and the subsequent invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq. Before joining the White House, she had been Provost of Stanford University (1993–1999) and a Professor of Political Science there, specializing in Soviet and Russian foreign and security policy. Her academic background shaped her approach to alliance management and great-power competition during her tenure at State.
Background and Career Path

Rice earned a bachelor’s degree in political science from the University of Denver in 1974, a master’s from Notre Dame in 1975, and a PhD from Denver’s Graduate School of International Studies in 1981 — focusing on the Soviet military and Czechoslovakia. She joined the National Security Council staff in 1989 under Brent Scowcroft during the George H.W. Bush administration, coordinating policy on the Soviet Union as communism collapsed. She returned to Stanford, then joined the 2000 Bush presidential campaign as a key foreign policy advisor.
Confirmation and Early Tenure

The January 18–19, 2005 confirmation hearings before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee were contentious. Senator Barbara Boxer (D-CA) issued the sharpest challenge, accusing Rice of “contradictions” and a “credibility gap” over statements made about Iraq’s weapons of mass destruction and the decision to invade. Despite opposition, the committee voted 16–2 to recommend her confirmation, with the full Senate confirming her 85–13 on January 26.

Rice’s early agenda as Secretary centered on repairing alliances strained by the Iraq War, particularly with France and Germany, which had opposed the 2003 invasion. Her first overseas trip in February 2005 included stops in London, Paris, Berlin, Warsaw, Ankara, Jerusalem, and Ramallah — a fourteen-day diplomatic blitz signaling that multilateral engagement would define her tenure. She also pushed for European unity on Iran’s nuclear program, helping to establish the EU3+US diplomatic framework that would evolve into the broader P5+1 talks.
Significance

Rice’s appointment represented a watershed in African American representation at the highest levels of American government. She served until January 20, 2009 — nearly a full four-year term — making her one of the longer-serving Secretaries of State of the early 21st century. Her tenure encompassed the January 2005 Iraqi elections, the Cedar Revolution in Lebanon, North Korea nuclear negotiations, and the beginning of Israeli-Palestinian peace efforts. Her confirmation occurred in a year of intense scrutiny of U.S. foreign policy and American identity, the same year Rosa Parks died (October 24, 2005), connecting Rice’s milestone to a longer arc of African American advancement in public life.

After leaving office, Rice returned to Stanford as a professor and senior fellow at the Hoover Institution. She also served on the Board of Directors of Chevron Corporation, Transamerica Corporation, and Hewlett-Packard.

text: Key figures: W. Mark Felt (former Associate Director of the FBI), John D. O’Connor (attorney and author of the Vanity Fair article), Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein (Washington Post reporters), Ben Bradlee (Washington Post executive editor during Watergate), Joan Felt (Felt’s daughter)
Summary

On May 31, 2005, the magazine Vanity Fair published an article by the California attorney John D. O’Connor titled “I’m the Guy They Called Deep Throat,” revealing that W. Mark Felt — who had served as the Associate Director, or second-ranking official, of the Federal Bureau of Investigation during the Watergate era — was the confidential source known as “Deep Throat.” For more than thirty years the source’s identity had been one of the most closely guarded secrets in American journalism and the subject of persistent guessing among historians, journalists, and former officials.

Felt, who was 91 years old and in declining health at the time of the disclosure, had helped guide Washington Post reporter Bob Woodward through the early reporting on the 1972 break-in at the Democratic National Committee headquarters in the Watergate complex and the ensuing cover-up. The scandal ultimately forced the resignation of President Richard Nixon in August 1974. Within hours of the Vanity Fair story, Woodward, his reporting partner Carl Bernstein, and former Post executive editor Ben Bradlee confirmed that Felt had indeed been their source.
The Secret Source

During the Watergate investigation, Woodward relied on a high-level government source whom he had promised to protect and to quote only on “deep background” — a category of sourcing in which information can be used but not attributed. The Post’s managing editor, Howard Simons, gave the source the nickname “Deep Throat,” a play on the deep-background arrangement and the title of a widely publicized 1972 pornographic film. In the reporters’ 1974 book All the President’s Men and the 1976 film adaptation, Deep Throat was portrayed meeting Woodward in a darkened Arlington, Virginia, parking garage, signaling meetings by moving a flowerpot and marking a newspaper. The film’s famous injunction to “follow the money” became emblematic of the story, though it does not appear in the book and is not documented as Felt’s actual words.

Woodward and Bernstein had pledged to keep the source’s identity confidential until his death or until he consented to be named. That commitment held for more than three decades, sustaining a long-running parlor game in Washington in which figures ranging from White House aides to intelligence officials were proposed as candidates. Felt himself repeatedly denied being Deep Throat over the years.
Motives and Controversy

Felt’s role prompted immediate debate over his motives. A career FBI official, he had been passed over for the directorship after J. Edgar Hoover’s death in May 1972, when Nixon installed the acting director L. Patrick Gray. Some observers cast Felt as an institutional defender of the FBI’s independence against White House interference in the Watergate inquiry; others viewed his cooperation with a reporter as driven partly by personal ambition and resentment. The disclosure reopened questions about the ethics of leaking, the use of anonymous sources, and the proper relationship between law-enforcement officials and the press.

Felt’s own record complicated the portrait of a straightforward whistleblower. In 1980 he was convicted of having authorized illegal FBI break-ins during the 1970s against associates of the radical Weather Underground; President Ronald Reagan pardoned him in 1981. The decision to go public in 2005 came from Felt’s family — including his daughter, Joan Felt — who, according to the Vanity Fair account, encouraged the aging Felt to claim his place in history and hoped the revelation might yield income from a book or film. The article preempted Woodward, who had prepared his own account and published the book The Secret Man weeks later.
Significance

The unmasking of Deep Throat resolved the most famous unanswered question of the Watergate saga and closed a chapter in the history of American investigative journalism. It renewed public attention to the role that a single, well-placed confidential source can play in holding power to account, and to the enduring tension between government secrecy and press freedom. Felt’s story was later dramatized in the 2017 film Mark Felt: The Man Who Brought Down the White House. Felt died on December 18, 2008, at the age of 95, three and a half years after the secret he had kept for a generation was finally revealed.

text: Key figures: Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, George Weah, Charles Gyude Bryant (transitional leader), Leymah Gbowee
Summary

On November 23, 2005, Ellen Johnson Sirleaf was declared the winner of the Liberian presidential election, becoming the first woman ever elected head of state on the African continent. Her victory came in a runoff held on November 8, 2005, in which she defeated former professional footballer George Weah with 59.40 percent of the vote (478,526 ballots) to Weah’s 40.60 percent (327,046 ballots). She was inaugurated as the 24th President of Liberia on January 16, 2006.

The elections were conducted under the framework of the Accra Comprehensive Peace Agreement of 2003, which had ended Liberia’s Second Civil War (1999–2003). A transitional government headed by Charles Gyude Bryant had administered the country in the interim. The two-round contest drew significant international attention: the first round on October 11, 2005, saw Weah lead with 28.27 percent and Sirleaf place second with 19.75 percent, among 22 candidates. No candidate secured the required majority, triggering the runoff. Voter turnout was 74.86 percent in the first round and 61.04 percent in the runoff.

International observers from the United Nations, European Union, Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), and the Carter Center monitored both rounds. The Carter Center reported only minor irregularities and found no evidence of the systematic fraud alleged by the Weah campaign. Weah formally withdrew his protest and conceded on December 22, 2005.
Background: Ellen Johnson Sirleaf

Ellen Eugenia Johnson Sirleaf was born on October 29, 1938, in Monrovia, Liberia. She studied at the College of West Africa and at Madison Business College in Wisconsin before earning a Bachelor of Arts in Economics from the University of Colorado Boulder and a Master of Public Administration from Harvard University’s Kennedy School of Government in 1971.

She entered Liberian government service, eventually rising to Finance Minister under President William Tolbert (1979–1980). After the April 1980 military coup led by Master Sergeant Samuel Doe, she fled the country and worked at the World Bank in Washington, D.C., and as Vice President of Citibank’s African Regional Office in Nairobi, Kenya (1981–1985). She returned to Liberia to contest a Senate seat in 1985, was arrested for criticising the Doe government, and was later released. In 1992, she joined the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), where she served as Director of the Regional Bureau for Africa and as an Assistant Secretary-General of the United Nations — the first woman to lead the UNDP’s Africa program. She resigned in 1997 to contest the presidency but lost to Charles Taylor, receiving approximately 10 percent of the vote against Taylor’s 75 percent.
The 2005 Campaign

Sirleaf ran as the candidate of the Unity Party on a platform of national reconciliation, economic reconstruction, and anti-corruption reform. She leveraged her international finance experience — at Harvard, Citibank, the World Bank, and the UNDP — to present herself as uniquely qualified to rebuild Liberia’s shattered institutions and attract foreign investment. Her opponent George Weah, a former FIFA World Player of the Year and African footballer of the year, was enormously popular but lacked formal education in governance, an issue Sirleaf and international commentators raised during the campaign.

In the first round, Weah’s strong popular support placed him first. However, Sirleaf built a winning coalition in the runoff, drawing support from urban educated voters, women’s groups energised by the peace activism of figures such as Leymah Gbowee, and voters who prioritised economic competency over celebrity appeal. Turnout remained high given the country’s recent history of conflict and the logistical challenges of post-war infrastructure.
Significance

Ellen Johnson Sirleaf’s election broke a historic barrier: no woman had previously been elected to lead an African nation. Her victory was widely interpreted as evidence that post-conflict democratic reconstruction could produce both free elections and transformative representation. As president from 2006 to 2018, she secured debt relief and foreign investment that helped stabilise Liberia’s economy, established a Truth and Reconciliation Commission, and worked to reintegrate former combatants.

In 2011, Sirleaf was jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize alongside compatriot Leymah Gbowee and Yemeni activist Tawakkol Karman. The Nobel Committee cited their “non-violent struggle for the safety of women and for women’s rights to full participation in peace-building work.” Her election in November 2005 thus stands as both a milestone for African democratic governance and for women’s political representation globally, coming the same year that Angela Merkel became Germany’s first female Chancellor and Condoleezza Rice became the first African American woman to serve as U.S. Secretary of State.

text: Key figures: Evo Morales, Jorge Quiroga, Samuel Doria Medina, Carlos Mesa, Eduardo Rodríguez Veltzé
Summary

On December 18, 2005, Juan Evo Morales Ayma, leader of the Movement for Socialism (Movimiento al Socialismo, MAS), was elected President of Bolivia with 1,544,374 votes, or 53.74 percent of the valid vote. His victory made him the first Bolivian head of state drawn from the country’s indigenous majority and the first candidate to win an absolute majority in a presidential election since the disputed contest of 1978. Because Morales cleared the 50 percent threshold, no congressional runoff was required — a departure from the practice, common in earlier Bolivian elections, of having the legislature choose among the leading candidates. He was inaugurated on January 22, 2006, for a five-year term.

His nearest rival, former president Jorge Quiroga of the conservative Social Democratic Power (Poder Democrático y Social, Podemos), took 821,745 votes (28.59 percent). The cement magnate Samuel Doria Medina of the National Unity Front finished third with 224,090 votes (7.80 percent). Turnout was high at 84.50 percent of registered voters. In the concurrent legislative elections, MAS won a majority in the Chamber of Deputies, taking 72 of 130 seats, while falling short in the Senate, where it held 12 of 36 seats to Podemos’s 13.
Background

The election was held early. President Carlos Mesa had resigned in June 2005 amid sustained protests over control of Bolivia’s natural gas reserves — the culmination of the unrest known as the “gas war” that had already forced the resignation of President Gonzalo Sánchez de Lozada in October 2003. Supreme Court Chief Justice Eduardo Rodríguez Veltzé assumed the presidency on an interim basis and called elections for December 2005, moving forward a vote that had been scheduled for 2007. The campaign unfolded against a backdrop of deep polarisation between the highland indigenous and popular movements of the west and the wealthier, more conservative eastern lowland departments centred on Santa Cruz.
Evo Morales

Evo Morales was born on October 26, 1959, in Isallawi, in the Orinoca Canton of the Oruro Department, into an Aymara family of subsistence farmers. He moved to the Chapare region and became a coca grower (cocalero), rising through the ranks of the coca-growers’ unions and campaigning against United States–backed coca eradication programmes, which he framed as an assault on indigenous livelihoods and culture. He built a national profile as a union leader before taking over the Movement for Socialism as its standard-bearer in the late 1990s and contesting the 2002 presidential election, in which he finished a close second.
Significance

Morales’s election was widely reported around the world as a watershed for indigenous political representation in Latin America, coming in a country where people of indigenous descent make up a majority of the population yet had historically been excluded from the highest office. His platform combined resource nationalism — above all the promised nationalisation of the hydrocarbons sector, which his government carried out by decree in May 2006 — with pledges to rewrite the constitution and expand the political voice of indigenous communities. A new constitution refounding Bolivia as a “plurinational” state was approved by referendum in 2009.

His victory formed part of the broader “pink tide” of left-leaning governments elected across South America in the 2000s. Morales went on to serve as president from January 2006 until his resignation in November 2019 amid disputes over that year’s election. His 2005 win came the same year that Ellen Johnson Sirleaf became the first woman elected to lead an African nation and Angela Merkel became Germany’s first female Chancellor, part of a year in which several elections broke long-standing barriers of gender and ethnicity.

text: Key figures: Hunter S. Thompson, Ralph Steadman (illustrator collaborator), Jann Wenner (Rolling Stone founder/editor), Johnny Depp (friend and patron), Juan Thompson (son)
Life and Career

Hunter Stockton Thompson was born on July 18, 1937, in Louisville, Kentucky, into a working-class family. An adolescent with a passion for literature — he typed out entire novels by F. Scott Fitzgerald and Ernest Hemingway to absorb their style — Thompson enlisted in the U.S. Air Force in 1956 and served as a sports editor for a base newspaper before receiving an early discharge in 1958. He spent the late 1950s and early 1960s as a struggling freelance journalist in Puerto Rico, South America, and California, developing the immersive, first-person style that would become his signature.
Rise to Prominence: Hell’s Angels and Gonzo

Thompson’s breakthrough came with Hell’s Angels: The Strange and Terrible Saga of the Outlaw Motorcycle Gangs (1966), the result of a year spent riding with the infamous motorcycle club. The book attracted national attention and established him as a writer willing to dissolve the boundary between observer and participant. He coined the term “Gonzo journalism” in 1970 — derived from a Boston Globe piece by Bill Cardoso describing Thompson’s first-person account of the Kentucky Derby for Scanlan’s Monthly — to describe his method of immersive, subjective reporting where the writer becomes a character in the story.

His 1971 masterpiece Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas, serialized in Rolling Stone and illustrated by British artist Ralph Steadman, blended a drug-fueled road trip narrative with corrosive satire of American materialism and the death of the 1960s counterculture. The book opens with its famous line: “We were somewhere around Barstow, on the edge of the desert, when the drugs began to take hold.” It sold modestly at first but became a cult classic that endures as one of the most distinctive works of American literary journalism.
Political Coverage and Rolling Stone

Founder Jann Wenner gave Thompson an unprecedented platform at Rolling Stone, where he served as national affairs editor. His coverage of the 1972 presidential campaign — later collected in Fear and Loathing: On the Campaign Trail ‘72 — was a landmark of political journalism, blending biting analysis with personal narrative. Thompson famously called Edmund Muskie a “treacherous brain-damaged old water-head” and predicted Richard Nixon’s landslide victory months before mainstream journalists acknowledged the possibility. His campaign coverage inspired a generation of political writers.

He ran for Sheriff of Pitkin County, Colorado, on the “Freak Power” platform in 1970, losing narrowly but demonstrating his belief that political engagement extended beyond commentary. His Aspen compound, Owl Farm, became a gathering place for writers, politicians, and celebrities throughout the 1970s and 1980s.
Later Career and ESPN Column

In his final years, Thompson wrote a weekly column, Hey Rube, for ESPN’s website (espn.com), covering the intersection of sports, politics, and culture. The column gave him a new audience and a late-career platform for commentary on the Bush administration’s foreign policy, the 2003 Iraq War, and what he saw as the collapse of American civic life. He remained deeply politically engaged, expressing contempt for what he described as the criminalization of American politics.
Death

Thompson died on February 21, 2005, at Owl Farm in Woody Creek, Colorado (near Aspen), from a self-inflicted gunshot wound to the head. He was 67 years old. His son Juan Thompson discovered him and found a note he had titled “Football Season Is Over”, written on February 16 — five days before his death — that expressed his philosophy: “No More Games. No More Bombs. No More Walking. No More Fun. No More Swimming. 67. That is 17 years past 50. 17 more than I needed or wanted. Boring. I am always bitchy. No Fun — for anybody. 67. You are getting Greedy. Act your old age. Relax — This won’t hurt.”

Thompson had suffered significant physical decline in his final years: a broken leg from a ski accident in 2003, hip replacement surgery, and spinal pain that severely limited his mobility. He had spoken throughout his life about suicide as a rational choice and had frequently stated that he would not allow himself to deteriorate into helplessness.

His longtime friend and collaborator Johnny Depp, who had portrayed Thompson in Terry Gilliam’s 1998 film adaptation of Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas and spent considerable time at Owl Farm, paid for Thompson’s funeral. In August 2005, at a memorial ceremony attended by celebrities including Jack Nicholson, Bill Murray, John Kerry, and Sean Penn, Depp funded the firing of Thompson’s ashes from a custom cannon built atop a 153-foot tower in the shape of a double-thumbed fist — Thompson’s personal symbol — at Owl Farm. The cannon shot was accompanied by fireworks and a rendition of “Mr. Tambourine Man.” The event reportedly cost approximately $2.5 million, largely funded by Depp.
Literary Legacy and Influence
Thompson’s influence on American journalism and literature is substantial and enduring:

He permanently altered expectations for what first-person reporting could be, opening space for narrative nonfiction writers including Tom Wolfe, Joan Didion, and later writers of the immersive longform tradition.
His political criticism — particularly his analysis of Nixon and the Vietnam-era power structure — remains a touchstone for political writing that combines visceral engagement with systemic critique.

Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas has sold millions of copies and is routinely cited as one of the defining works of 20th-century American literature; it appeared in Modern Library’s readers’ list of the 100 best novels.
His personal style — the aviator glasses, cigarette holder, and tropical shirts — became iconic shorthand for a certain kind of American rebel intellectual.

Terry Gilliam’s 1998 film starring Johnny Depp and Benicio del Toro introduced Thompson to new generations, and a 2008 documentary, Gonzo: The Life and Work of Dr. Hunter S. Thompson, further cemented his legacy.

text: Key figures: Lance Armstrong, Ivan Basso (2nd place), Jan Ullrich (3rd place), George Hincapie, Levi Leipheimer, Johan Bruyneel (team director)
Summary

Lance Armstrong won his seventh consecutive Tour de France on July 24, 2005, crossing the finish line on the Champs-Élysées with a total race time of 86 hours, 15 minutes, 2 seconds — more than 4 minutes and 40 seconds ahead of second-place finisher Ivan Basso (Team CSC) and nearly 6 minutes ahead of third-place Jan Ullrich (T-Mobile). The 2005 Tour ran from July 2 to July 24 over 3,608 kilometers (2,242 miles) divided into 21 stages, including grueling alpine sections in the Pyrenees and Alps. Armstrong’s Discovery Channel team, directed by Belgian coach Johan Bruyneel, executed a near-flawless tactical campaign, protecting their leader through the mountain stages while launching decisive attacks when rivals were most vulnerable.

Born Lance Edward Gunderson on September 18, 1971, in Plano, Texas (later adopting the surname of his stepfather Terry Armstrong), Armstrong had been diagnosed with advanced testicular cancer in 1996 — a cancer that had spread to his brain, lungs, and abdomen. His remission and return to elite cycling made him one of sports’ most prominent comeback narratives. In 2005, at age 33, he became the oldest Tour de France winner since the 1920s.
The 2005 Tour: Race Narrative

Armstrong entered the 2005 Tour as a heavy favorite but faced pressure from Basso and a resurgent Ullrich. He did not win the prologue (that went to David Zabriskie) but took the yellow jersey after Stage 4 and never fully relinquished overall dominance. Key moments included:
Stage 10 (Courchevel): Armstrong cracked Basso on the final climb, opening a gap that proved decisive for overall classification.
Stage 11 (Briançon to Courchevel): Armstrong attacked solo on the final ascent, winning the stage and extending his lead to over 2 minutes over Basso.
Stage 20 (Time Trial, St-Étienne): Armstrong won the final individual time trial, adding further seconds to his lead and effectively sealing the overall victory.

He stood atop the podium at the traditional Champs-Élysées finish in Paris and announced his retirement from professional cycling at the post-race ceremony — a declaration he would eventually reverse in 2009 when he returned to race again.
The Livestrong Foundation

The 2005 victory amplified the profile of Armstrong’s cancer awareness charity, the Lance Armstrong Foundation (later rebranded Livestrong in 2012). Yellow Livestrong silicone wristbands — first produced in 2004 for the Athens Olympics — had by mid-2005 become a global phenomenon, with over 70 million wristbands sold. Proceeds funded cancer research programs and patient navigation services. The wristband popularized a broader trend of charity silicone bands across sports and cause marketing. Armstrong’s celebrity allowed Livestrong to expand its reach into schools, hospitals, and international health organizations during 2005.
Significance and Later Controversy

Armstrong’s seventh Tour victory made him a transcendent global sports figure whose story of illness and triumph resonated far beyond cycling audiences. His achievement attracted mainstream media coverage, celebrity sponsorships, and a White House visit. However, the win occurred against an increasingly turbulent backdrop: the French sports newspaper L’Équipe published a front-page investigation in August 2005 claiming that stored urine samples from Armstrong’s 1999 Tour de France victory had tested positive for EPO using a new detection method — allegations Armstrong denied.

The full reckoning came in October 2012, when the U.S. Anti-Doping Agency (USADA) released a 1,000-page report concluding that Armstrong had orchestrated “the most sophisticated, professionalized and successful doping program that sport has ever seen.” The International Cycling Union subsequently stripped Armstrong of all seven Tour titles, leaving the 2005 edition with no official winner. Armstrong publicly admitted to doping in a January 2013 television interview with Oprah Winfrey.

The rise and fall of Armstrong’s story shaped how sports media and anti-doping authorities approached athlete testing and narrative accountability for a generation. In 2005, though, he remained the celebrated face of cycling and a global symbol of athletic resilience — a cultural context shared with major events of that year including Hurricane Katrina’s test of American fortitude and the confirmed achievement of Condoleezza Rice as Secretary of State, which together defined 2005 as a year of both landmark success stories and impending reckonings.

text: Key figures: Mahmoud Abbas (Abu Mazen), Mustafa Barghouti, Yasser Arafat (predecessor), Ariel Sharon (Israeli PM), Jimmy Carter (international observer), Joe Biden (U.S. Senate observer)
Summary

On January 9, 2005, Mahmoud Abbas was elected President of the Palestinian Authority, winning 501,448 votes — 67.38 percent — in a field of seven candidates. His closest challenger, independent physician and activist Mustafa Barghouti, received 156,227 votes (20.99 percent). Turnout was 73.42 percent of the roughly 1.09 million registered voters across the West Bank, Gaza Strip, and East Jerusalem. The election was the first Palestinian presidential contest since Yasser Arafat’s unopposed re-election in 1996 and was called following Arafat’s death in Paris on November 11, 2004, at age 75. Hamas and Islamic Jihad boycotted the contest, citing what they called a premature political process. Abbas was inaugurated on January 15, 2005, at the Palestinian Authority’s headquarters in Ramallah.

Abbas — known by his kunya Abu Mazen — was born in Safed in 1935 and fled during the 1948 Arab-Israeli war, eventually becoming one of the founding members of Fatah in the late 1950s alongside Arafat. A trained lawyer with a doctorate from the Oriental University in Moscow (1982), he was regarded within the PLO as its chief negotiator and served as the lead Palestinian signatory to the 1993 Oslo Accords. He had previously served as the Palestinian Authority’s first prime minister from March to September 2003, a post created under pressure from the United States and the Quartet (the U.S., European Union, Russia, and United Nations) as part of the Roadmap for Peace. His first term ended after less than six months amid public clashes with Arafat over control of security forces.

After Arafat’s death, Abbas was named PLO chairman by the organization’s Executive Committee and was subsequently endorsed as Fatah’s presidential candidate by the movement’s Revolutionary Council on November 25, 2004. The 2005 election was monitored by more than 900 international observers, including a delegation led by former U.S. President Jimmy Carter, U.S. Senators Joe Biden and John Sununu, and a European Union mission. The EU characterized the vote as “a very important step towards the creation of a viable and democratic Palestinian state.”
Campaign Platform and Political Context

Abbas campaigned explicitly on ending the Second Intifada, which had claimed roughly 3,000 Palestinian and 1,000 Israeli lives since September 2000, and on resuming direct negotiations with Israel. He called for a negotiated two-state solution and consistently rejected armed operations against Israeli civilians — a stance that distinguished him sharply from more militant factions within Fatah itself. He pledged reform of Palestinian Authority institutions, including consolidation of the fragmented security services that had proliferated under Arafat, and promised to crack down on financial corruption that had long plagued the PA.

His election came weeks after President George W. Bush had named the Israeli-Palestinian conflict a priority for his second term (see George W. Bush’s 2005 agenda) and days before Secretary of State-designate Condoleezza Rice’s confirmation hearings (see Rice as Secretary of State). The incoming Bush administration signaled greater willingness to engage the Palestinian leadership under Abbas than it had under Arafat, and Abbas’s victory was welcomed by Washington as an opening for diplomacy.
Sharm el-Sheikh and the Gaza Disengagement

On February 8, 2005, Abbas met Israeli Prime Minister Ariel Sharon at the Sharm el-Sheikh Summit in Egypt — the first formal summit between Palestinian and Israeli leaders since the collapse of Camp David in July 2000. The two leaders declared a mutual cessation of violence, with Abbas pledging to prevent Palestinian attacks on Israelis and Sharon pledging to halt Israeli military operations against Palestinians. Although the ceasefire was fragile and repeatedly tested by rocket fire from Gaza and Israeli targeted killings, it broadly held through the summer.

The summit set the stage for Israel’s unilateral disengagement from the Gaza Strip, announced by Sharon and carried out in August–September 2005, during which Israel evacuated all 21 Israeli settlements in Gaza and four in the northern West Bank, withdrawing approximately 9,000 settlers (see Gaza Disengagement). Abbas accepted the handover of Gaza, which the Palestinian Authority formally received on September 12, 2005. The Rafah border crossing between Gaza and Egypt was reopened to Palestinian travelers in November 2005 under a European Union monitoring mission (EU BAM Rafah), a direct product of the diplomacy that Abbas’s election had enabled.
Palestinian Political Divisions

Abbas’s election papered over a deepening rift within Palestinian politics. Hamas, which had boycotted the presidential election, performed strongly in Palestinian municipal elections held in January and May 2005. In January 2006, Hamas would win a parliamentary majority in Palestinian Legislative Council elections — a result that triggered an international funding cutoff to the PA and ultimately led to the violent takeover of Gaza by Hamas in June 2007, splitting Palestinian governance between a Fatah-run West Bank Authority and a Hamas-controlled Gaza Strip.

Abbas’s authority was thus circumscribed almost from the beginning of his mandate. His four-year presidential term formally expired in January 2009; when no new election was held, Abbas issued a decree extending his own term indefinitely. As of the mid-2020s, no subsequent Palestinian presidential election has taken place, making his January 2005 mandate the foundation of nearly two decades of continuous rule.
Significance

Abbas’s election marked the first internationally recognized, orderly transfer of power in Palestinian Authority history — a legitimizing moment that opened a brief diplomatic window. It came at a pivotal juncture: Israel’s planned unilateral Gaza withdrawal gave Abbas a tangible political achievement to show Palestinians, while U.S. and European engagement provided financial and diplomatic support. The election’s legacy is deeply contested: it produced real diplomatic progress in 2005, including the Sharm el-Sheikh ceasefire and the Gaza handover, but the subsequent Palestinian split undermined his authority and the two-state process neither side had been able to close.

Key figures: Michael Jackson (defendant), Judge Rodney Melville, prosecutor Tom Sneddon (Santa Barbara County District Attorney), defense attorneys Thomas Mesereau Jr. and Susan Yu, Gavin Arvizo (accuser), jury foreperson Paul Rodriguez
Summary

Michael Jackson was acquitted on June 13, 2005, of all fourteen charges in one of the most heavily covered celebrity trials in American history. The verdict came after a five-month trial at the Santa Barbara County courthouse in Santa Maria, California, capping a legal saga that had begun with Jackson’s arrest in November 2003.
Background and charges

The prosecution centered on Gavin Arvizo, a 13-year-old cancer survivor who had appeared in a Martin Bashir documentary about Jackson’s Neverland Ranch in February 2003. Santa Barbara County District Attorney Tom Sneddon, who had investigated Jackson over unproven allegations in 1993, filed a 10-count indictment in April 2004. The charges included four counts of lewd and lascivious acts with a minor under 14, one count of attempted lewd act, four counts of administering an intoxicating agent (alcohol) to a minor, and one count of conspiracy covering extortion, child abduction, and false imprisonment of the Arvizo family.
Trial proceedings (January–June 2005)

Jury selection concluded January 28, 2005, and opening statements began on January 31. The prosecution called 82 witnesses over roughly ten weeks, presenting testimony about events at Neverland in February and March 2003. Defense attorney Thomas Mesereau mounted an aggressive cross-examination strategy, attacking the credibility of the Arvizo family and presenting witnesses who testified that Gavin had made similar accusations in the past. Jackson attended all 61 days of testimony — sometimes visibly unwell, arriving in pajama bottoms on one occasion after being hospitalized for a back injury.

The jury of eight women and four men received the case on June 3, 2005, and deliberated for approximately 32 hours across seven days. On June 13 they returned unanimous verdicts of not guilty on all 10 original counts and all four lesser-included charges.
Aftermath

Jackson emerged from the courthouse to cheers from thousands of supporters who had camped outside throughout the trial. He subsequently traveled to Bahrain as a guest of Sheikh Abdullah, effectively beginning a period of self-imposed exile from the United States that lasted until 2006. Santa Barbara County had spent an estimated $3.5 million prosecuting the case. Jackson’s defense was reported to have cost more than $5 million.
Significance

The acquittal was a landmark in celebrity jurisprudence. District Attorney Sneddon had pursued Jackson publicly for over a decade, and the not-guilty verdict was widely interpreted as a rebuke of what critics called an overzealous prosecution. At the same time, the trial permanently damaged Jackson’s commercial standing: album sales and licensing deals had slowed dramatically since his 2003 arrest, and the reputational cost outlasted the legal one.

The case sharpened debate about media saturation of high-profile trials — court television networks devoted near-continuous coverage — and about whether celebrity defendants could receive fair proceedings. Jury foreperson Paul Rodriguez said afterward that the jurors found the Arvizo family’s testimony inconsistent and not credible beyond a reasonable doubt, illustrating how prosecutorial credibility is often the decisive variable in complex child-abuse cases.

Jackson’s death on June 25, 2009, reignited public interest in the allegations. The 2019 HBO documentary Leaving Neverland, featuring two men who claimed Jackson had abused them as children in earlier years, prompted a new wave of debate that continues to shape how his musical legacy is assessed — demonstrating that a not-guilty verdict does not permanently settle public opinion.
